title: SignalFrame: Founder Story Podcast + Case Study Recording
summary: Podcast-style interview capturing SignalFrame's product journey using Redwood Inference for real-time creative personalization. Covers deployment choice, measurable latency/cost wins, go-to-market impact, and a few security/compliance notes. Recording will seed a written case study and a short social clip.
topics: Origin story: why SignalFrame built personalization at scale
Why Redwood: latency, deterministic pricing, private deployment options
Implementation: Dedicated vs Hosted tradeoffs, KV cache, streaming
Results: latency reductions, cost per request, launch velocity
Operational notes: SOC 2, SSO, audit logs, and internal adoption
transcript:
Header: 2026-10-21 16:00 PT | Duration: ~42m | Recording: Zoom (podcast studio)
Attendees: Samira P. (Redwood), Liam O. (Redwood AE), Asha K. (Founder), Diego M. (CTO)

[00:00] Samira (Redwood): Hey everyone, welcome to the Redwood customer spotlight. We have Asha and Diego from SignalFrame. Thanks for joining, super excited.
[00:08] Asha (SignalFrame): Thanks Samira, great to be here — excited to talk about the messy early days, uh, and the good days now.
[00:15] Liam (Redwood): Quick note, we'll do audio and then we might pull a 60s clip for socials. Asha, maybe start with a quick one-minute origin story for listeners.
[00:24] Asha: Sure — SignalFrame started as a video-first creative platform, we wanted dynamic scenes that change per viewer, and to do that at scale we needed generative models in the render loop. Early on we built custom infra, which, surprise, was expensive and fragile, right? We hit cost spikes when sequences got longer and memory blowouts on our GPUs.
[00:42] Diego: And to add, our cache strategy was naive; we'd re-run prompts for small variants — we'd seen 2-3x cost variability week-to-week.
[00:52] Samira: Nice — so where did Redwood come in? What were the key decision points?
[00:58] Asha: For us it was predictability. Redwood's Dedicated offering — or as the engineering team called it 'Redwood Dedicted' for a while — gave a predictable throughput and the SLOs were easier to reason about. Also the KV cache and continuous batching features were huge, they let us re-use context across viewers.
[01:18] Diego: The runtime's batching and kernel selection reduced tail latency. Before Redwood we had 900-1,200ms p95 on a certain flow; after tuning with Redwood we got to ~320-380ms p95, which was night-and-day for UX.
[01:33] Samira: Wow, that's a big drop. Any funny or surprising part of the integration?
[01:37] Asha: Ha — we thought we would need deep model surgery. Instead Redwood recommended a smaller quantized variant for the high-volume path and a higher-quality hosted variant for canary users. That hybrid approach cut costs and kept fidelity for paid tiers.
[01:50] Liam: Right, and the model routing/fallback features let them avoid blackouts during busy drops.
[01:55] Diego: One small hiccup was labels in the console — the team typoed 'throughput units' as 'throughput points' which confused our finance folks for a week, but it was resolved.
[02:06] Samira: Haha, product-first problems. Let's talk security — our listeners will want to know: what controls mattered to you?
[02:13] Diego: SSO, RBAC, and audit logs were must-haves. We run in a regulated vertical for some clients so the private control plane option and KMS integration were decisive. The process took longer than a simple SaaS onboarding, but Redwood's solutions team was hands-on.
[02:30] Asha: Also, the ability to pin model versions during campaigns prevented surprising regressions — that was, honestly, a lifesaver after a bad open-source model patch we tried early on.
[02:40] Samira: Good callout. For metrics — can you share any public numbers you feel comfortable with?
[02:45] Asha: Sure. On average our per-request cost dropped ~40% after moving daytime traffic to a Redwood Dedicated pool and using caching aggressively. Latency at p95 dropped roughly 2.5x for the personalized render path. Launch velocity improved — what used to be a two-week infra project became two days of config.
[03:08] Liam: Those numbers matched the bench we ran during PoC — nice to see real-world confirmation.
[03:12] Samira: Speaking of PoC, walk us through how the pilot went.
[03:16] Diego: We started with a 3-week PoC: initial ingestion of prompts, run a small traffic slice on hosted, then escalate to dedicated for burst windows. Redwood's telemetry and trace hooks made it easier to find hotspots. There were a few transription-ish moments where node autoscaling lagged, but the rollback policy worked well.
[03:34] Samira: Any comments about the developer experience? Redwoods SDKs, docs — are they helpful?
[03:40] Asha: Docs were solid, but we did hit a few places where the sample for streaming responses didn't match our streaming library — small mismatch. The SDKs worked well overall and the community examples were helpful.
[03:52] Diego: I'd add the observability in the Console was probably the thing our PM loved the most — cost per token/route breakdowns saved several late-night calls.
[04:03] Samira: Love that. For the case study, are there any anecdotes or quotes you'd like us to pull out?
[04:09] Asha: Quote: 'Redwood let us stop babysitting infra and start shipping creative ideas.' Short and honest.
[04:17] Diego: Another tech quote: 'We went from reactive firefighting to workload owners who can tune cost vs. latency in minutes.'
[04:26] Samira: Excellent. We'll probably use one of those on the landing collateral. Quick pivot — how did product/marketing coordinate on rollout?
[04:33] Asha: We ran a beta cohort, had a joint dashboard for the first campaign, and used the eval harness Redwood suggested to detect quality regressions. That prevented a few awkward personalization moments.
[04:45] Samira: Did you test any competitor offerings as part of evaluation?
[04:49] Asha: We benchmarked a mix of managed endpoints and our own self-hosted stack. Competitors included Anthropic managed endpoints and a mix of cloud vendor GPU endpoints. Redwood's consistent perf/cost tradeoff and the private deployment option tipped the scales.
[05:03] Liam: Noted. Listeners often ask about long-term savings — do you feel the Dedicated model is worth the commit?
[05:08] Diego: For us, yes. We amortized the reserved capacity within 3 months because we run high-volume personalization during peak campaigns. The predictability in cost allowed finance to plan and freed up dev cycles.
[05:22] Samira: Any regrets or things you'd change?
[05:25] Asha: We should have involved product analytics earlier to instrument more fine-grained quality signals. We lost a week chasing a false positive in an A/B.
[05:34] Diego: I'd also say more early testing of extreme tail cases would have saved one big incident — large sequences plus dynamic assets stressed kv cache settings.
[05:45] Samira: Great transparency! Okay, lightning round — rapid fire: favorite Redwood feature?
[05:50] Asha: Caching suggestions and the rollout/rollback hooks.
[05:54] Diego: Console tracing per route.
[05:57] Liam: (laughs) I knew you'd say that. Favorite SignalFrame moment since launch?
[06:01] Asha: First time we saw user retention lift after personalized creative — we had a campaign live for 48 hours and saw a 7% uplift in CTR.
[06:08] Samira: Love that. We have about 36 minutes left — we'll shift into the deeper technical dive where we might pick at specifics, but still keep it podcast-y.
[06:19] [DEEP DIVE START]
[06:21] Diego: On the implementation, we used a two-path routing: fast-quantized models for anonymous viewers, higher-quality hosted for logged-in users. Redwood's fallback policy meant that if the dedicated pool warmed poorly we could route to hosted without changing the app.
[06:38] Samira: How did you manage KV cache sizes and eviction?
[06:42] Diego: We tuned TTLs per campaign and prioritized prefix caching. At first we kept everything for 10 minutes which is overkill; after telemetry we shortened to 60-90s for high churn segments, that kept accuracy and saved memory.
[06:56] Asha: Also happy note: the Redwood recommended batch sizes matched our seq length distribution; that removed a ton of manual tuning.
[07:05] Samira: Any shorthand for teams listening that want to try something similar?
[07:09] Asha: Start with a tiny beta, measure tail latency and cost per route, and be ruthless about telemetry. Also get security/compliance asks in week zero.
[07:20] Liam: We'll add a Redwood playbook link in the show notes — a how-to for personalization workloads.
[07:26] Samira: Perfect. Audience Q — someone asked about offline evals and regressions.
[07:31] Diego: We built a set of prompt-combo tests and ran nightly evals. When a model change caused a drift, our alerting flagged it and we pinned the previous version.
[07:41] Samira: Great operational maturity. Asha, any closing thoughts for product leaders listening?
[07:46] Asha: Don't be afraid to mix model qualities. You can get the best of both worlds — high fidelity for critical paths and much cheaper quantized paths for everything else. And pick partners who move quick with you.
[07:58] Samira: Awesome. We'll wrap in about 5 minutes — final logistics around the case study assets: Liam, what's the timeline?
[08:05] Liam: We'll draft a one-pager and a long-form case study copy. Plan: first draft by Oct 28, internal review by Oct 31, publish early Nov. Audio clip for socials edited by Nov 5.
[08:18] Asha: That timeline works for us, just flag anything with client-sensitive metrics and we'll sign off.
[08:24] Samira: Perfect. Last few minutes: any off-script fun facts? Asha, any hobbies?
[08:29] Asha: (laughs) I make short films on weekends — some of the personalization ideas actually came from experimental shorts.
[08:35] Diego: Heh, and I break infra in new and interesting ways on purpose sometimes.
[08:40] Samira: Love it. Okay that's a wrap — thank you both so much. We'll follow up with the draft case study and the edit pass.
[08:49] Asha: Thanks everyone!
[08:51] Liam: Appreciate it — thanks.

[END] Note: Some timestamps are approximate and a few words may be transcribed imperfectly (e.g., 'Dedicted' in place of 'Dedicated', 'kv' vs 'KV cache', small acronyms mis-typed).
